Title:
 Standard Test Method for Determination of 
 water 
 in Insulating oil.
Introduction

This document outlines the 
 testing procedure P1, which must be performed 
 on an annually bases 
 as indicated by Y1 in the above title block and 
may be subject to be changed according to directives of 
Central Chemical Laboratories.

This document applies for 
 the determination of water in new and used insulating oils over the 
 concentration range 2 mg/kg to 100 mg/kg. The precision data apply only to 
 new oils with viscosity less than 20 mm2/s at 40C.
Note 1:

For used oils, the accuracy of the method may be 
affected by the presence of contaminants and degradation products.

The experimental details of the method have been 
designed to be particularly suitable for mineral oils complying with IEC 
publication 296: specification for new insulating oils for transformers and 
switchgear. For use with other oils, modifications to the solvent proportions or 
sample size may be required.

sections.text: Summary of Test Method

A chloroform-methanol mixture is introduced into the titration vessel and 
 the water in this solvent mixture is reacted with karl fiscker reagent.

The 
 sample is then added to the solvent and the mixture again titrated with karl 
 fischer reagent. The sample is then added to the solvent and the mixture 
 again titrated with karl 
 fischer reagent. The karl fischer reagent is standardized against an 
 accurately metered amount of water. The end-point of the titration is 
 detected electrometrically using platinum electrodes immersed in the 
 solution across which a specified potential difference is applied. The 
 presence of water in the titration mixture causes polarization of the 
 cathode, thus opposing the passage of current. At the end-point of the 
 titration, excess karl fischer reagent depolarizes the cathode giving an 
 increase in current which is shown on a microammeter in series with the 
 electrodes.
Chemistry

The method is based on the reaction of water with a 
solution of iodine and sulphur dioxide in a pyridine-methanol mixture (karl 
fischer reagent).

Actual reactions are complex, but are essentially of water with iodine and 
sulphur dioxide and may be expressed as:

H2O + I2 + SO2 + 3C5H5N
→ 2C5H5N.HI + C5H5N.SO3

C5H5N
 SO3 
+ CH3OH → C5H5NH.SO4.CH3

Note 2 : 
 Pyridine can be replaced by other 
chemicals to control the pH during the reaction.
Safety Precautions

The sample must be taken as MPIS - procedure No 
 TD-SS-003-r0.

Make sure the sample bottle is correctly 
 labled.

Clean all glassware by removing any residual oil 
 with an appropriate solvent.

Solvents 
 like methyl ethyl ketone are flammable so keep it 
 away from heat, sparks, and open flame, keep container closed, use only with 
 adequate ventilation, avoid prolonged breathing of vapor or spray mist, 
 avoid prolonged or repeated contact with skin.

Solvents 
 like chromic acid (cleaning solution) is danger causes severe burns. A 
 recognized carcinogenic. Strong oxidizer, contact with other material may 
 cause fire. Hygroscopic, don't get in eyes, on skin or on clothing. Don't 
 take internally. Wash thoroughly after handling. keep container closed, use with adequate 
 ventilation,

sections.text:
Tools 
and Equipment

Reagents and Auxiliary 
Materials

items:
Karl fischer reagent, water equivalent 2.5 mg water / ml to 5 mg water/ ml, 
 approximately (see note 1)

Methanol, analytical reagent grade, water content approximately 0.05% (see 
 note2)

Chloroform, analytical reagent grade, water content approximately 0.05% (see 
 note2)
Magnesium perchlorate, dried, used as desiccant.

Lubricating grease, polytetrafluoroethlene filled petroleum or fluorinated 
 hydrocarbon types.

Some batches of karl fischer reagent may not be suitable because they do not 
 show the very rapid increase in the electrode current referred to in the 
 note of Procedure.

A small quantity of water has to be present in the solvent for the reaction to 
 proceed satisfactorily. The reagent qualities specified have been found 
 suitable, but should not be further dried.

Warning! Certain reagents may be detrimental to human health and must be 
 handled with proper care.

sections.text: Apparatus (See Figures 1,2,3 and 4)

Note 4: 
 Particular attention should be paid to cock 8 . 
 During use, the solvent action of Karl Fisher reagent on the grease 
 gradually creates an ungreased path between the ports of the cock, allowing 
 direct transfer of reagent between the reservoir and the titration vessel. 
 This effect, although small, can lead to significant errors, and can be 
 minimized by maintaining the liquid levels in the reservoir and the 
 titration vessel at approximately the same height, and also by regular 
 greasing of the cock.

electrometric titration apparatus
Figure 2 Suitable burette jet

 3 Details of electrodes construction

items:
Flanged titration vessel, nominal 250 ml capacity, inside diameter 50 mm. A 
 drainage tap fitted to the base is an advantage when the vessel is to be 
 emptied. The titration vessel should be shielded from direct sunlight when in 
 use.

Titration vessel lid, flanged to match the titration vessel, with at least four 
 sockets, one of which should be at least a conical ground joint 14/23 to 
 facilitate the addition of solid samples. One socket should be fitted with a 
 rubber septum.

Note 5: The electrode is particularly robust when 1mm diameter wire is used and has 
 been designed for use also with solid samples. If, however, only liquid 
 samples are to be tested, the free end of the wire need not be anchored and 
 smaller diameter wire may be used.The distance between the electrode wires is unimportant but care should be 
 taken, when using small diameter wire, to prevent accidental short-circuiting. 
 If anchored loops are made, the maximum width of the loops should not exceed 5 
 mm to allow the electrode assembly to pass through a conical joint 10/19.The electrode current at the inflexion point of the sensitivity curve is 
 mainly determined by the surface area of the cathode and to a much smaller 
 extent by the stirring speed. A suitable surface area is obtained by forming 
 loops of inside diameter 2.2 mm for 1 mm diameter wire. The table in Figure 3 
 gives, for various diameters of wire, the lengths of exposed wire required to 
 give the same surface area. Other values can be found by interpolation

Figure 
 3 Details of electrodes construction

Reservoir for Karl Fischer reagent, black-painted or brown glass of suitable 
 capacity.

Electrometric circuit as shown in Figure 4.
 Note 7: Commercial instruments may use proprietary circuiting. 
 These can be used provided their sensitivity and performance are not worse 
 than indicated in this standard.
Drying tubes for titration vessel and reagent reservoir.

Syringes should be dismantled and washed free of 
 traces of previous samples, either with a suitable detergent solution, soapy 
 water or a chlorinated hydrocarbon solvent, depending on the nature of the 
 samples, rinsed thoroughly with warm water, then deionized water and finally, 
 after draining, with methanol. Dry the clean syringes in a well-ventilated 
 oven at 115 5C for at least 1h, then 
 cool to room temperature in a desiccator.

Karl Fischer apparatus: ensure that all joints 
 in glassware and tubing are properly made and lightly coated with grease (see 
 note of Figure 1). Check that the stirrer bar in the titration vessel will not 
 contact the burette jet tip or electrodes when revolved. Fit the Karl Fischer 
 solution reservoir to the burette and check that the desiccant in all drying 
 tubes is in good condition, i.e. white and crystalline. (The desiccant will 
 normally require changing at least every fourteen days).

sections.text: Work to be Carried Out

items:
Fill the burette with Karl Fischer reagent, 
 then empty it back into the reservoir. Swirl the content of the reservoir 
 gently but thoroughly, taking care not to impose any strain on the glass 
 tubing connections. Repeat this procedure three more times; the burette will 
 now be dry and the reagent
 homogeneous. Refill the burette.

Turn tap 8 (see Figure 1) to connect 
 the burette to the jet and flush the jet with the contents of the burette. 
 Discard the reagent in the titration vessel and refill the burette to the zero 
 graduation.

Add 75 ml of chloroform-methanol mixture (1:1 
 by volume) to the titration vessel.

Switch on the magnetic stirrer, and adjust to 
 a speed within the range mentioned in item 5) of Apparatus 1.

With the three-way switch in posirion A 
 (Figure 4), adjust the "Millivolts control" to give a microammeter 
 reading of 100 μA (equivalent to a circuit 
 potential of 200 mV).

With the switch in position B, titrate the 
 solvent mixture in the titration vessel with Karl Fischer reagent until the 
 microammeter maintains a resonably steady reading of about 50 μA. Switch to 
 position C and continue titrating until the microammeter maintains a mean 
 reading of 70 5 μA which does not drop 
 more than 2 μA in 4 min. Note the meter reading, allowing for any oscillations 
 that may occur. Fill the burette to the zero graduation. 
 Note 8: During the initial stage of the titration of the 
 residual water in the solvent, addition of Karl Fischer reagent causes a 
 very rapid increase in the electrode current, followed by a fairly rapid 
 fall. As the titration progresses, the current fluctuations becomes much 
 less rapid and the rotary 
 switch can be turned to position C.
 With some electrodes, the current at the end-point may oscillate around a mean 
 value by up to 2 μA. The titration 
 should be continued until this mean value is 70 5 
 μA, (i.e. the mean value should be between 65 μA and 75 μA, disregarding the 
 oscillations) and the downward drift of the mean value is less than 2 μA in 4 
 min.

With samples which have been collected in glass 
 bottles, fill a syringe with oil, keeping the tip of the canulla well 
 below the surface of the oil. Replace the top of the glass bottle immediately. 
 Hold the syringe vertically, with the cannula uppermost, discharge all air 
 bubbles and discard the contents of the syringe. Refill the syringe and weigh 
 to the nearest 0.1 g. With samples which have been collected in a syringe, 
 discharge approximately 2 ml to flush out the canulla and weigh the syringe 
 to the nearest 0.1 g.

Inject a quantity of oil into the titration 
 vessel via the septum cap and re-weigh the syringe. Record the mass M, in grams, of sample injected. The quantity of oil injected may be 
 varied according to the approximate moisture content of the oil, if known. A 
 range of 5 g to 25 g is suggested.

Titrate the moisture with Karl 
 Fischer reagent until the microammeter needle remains at the reading noted in 
 6. Record the volume a in millilitres

Carry out a duplicate determination by emptying 
 the titration vessel and repeating the steps described in 3 and 
 6 to 9.

Without emptying the vessel after the second 
 determination, proceed immediately with the standardization of the Karl 
 Fischer reagent as described in (Standardization of Karl Fischer Reagent).
Refill the burette to the zero position.

Fill a 10 μl chromatographic syringe with 
 deionized water.

Inject the water into the titration vessel, 
 taking care not to depress the plunger of the syringe while passing the needle 
 through the septum cap. Submerge the needle tip below the surface of the 
 liquid mixture before injection of the water. Record the quantity of water 
 injected in milligrams

Titrate with Karl Fischer mixture until the 
 microammeter needle remains at the reading noted in the procedure (6). Record the 
 volume b in millilitres.

sections.text: mg of water added

items:
b = millilitres of Karl Fischer reagent used in Standardization of Karl Fischer Reagent
 (4).

a = millilitres of Karl Fischer reagent used in the 
 procedure (9),
 W = water equivalent of Karl Fischer reagent,
 M = mass, in grammes, of the sample injected in the procedure (8).

sections.text: Report

Report the water content of the oil sample as the 
 average of the duplicate determinations to the nearest integer in milligrammes 
 of water per kilogramme oil.
Repeatability

Duplicate determinations carried out by one operator should be considered 
 suspect at the 95% confidence level if they differ by more than 0.77 √ X 
 mg/kg (where X is the average of the duplicate determinations).
Reproducibility

When two laboratories test different samples of the same oil, each will 
 produce duplicate results and report their average.The two averages should not be considered suspect at the 95% confidence 
 level unless they differ by more than 3.25 √X mg/kg (where X is the average 
 of the two averages).

Note: The 
 electronic circuit is a simple amperometric circuit with the microammeter in 
 series with the electrodes. The microammeter should have a low internal 
 resistance in order to give high sensitivity. A value of about 300Ώ 
 has been found suitable.

When the circuit is switched 
 on, approximately 300 mV is developed across the 100Ώ potentiometer. With the 
 rotary switch in position A, and the potentiometer adjusted to give full 
 scale deflection on the microammeter, 200 mV is supplied to the electrode 
 circuit. With the three-way switch in position B, resistor R is connected in 
 series with the microammeter to protect the microammeter movement from 
 damage caused by violent current fluctuations which can occur during 
 the initial stages of the titration.

4 Circuit for the electrometric detection of the 
end-point

extraction tube
Figure 6 Current / potential curves

Figure 7 Sensitivity of
